question: What does a slow introduction promise, and what does the Vivace make of it?
intro: A slow introduction with a passing shadow of G minor opens the symphony, then comes to rest in a hush before a rapid 6/8 Vivace. The exposition offers several thematic characters; listen for how the opening motif is then worked through the development and returns.

sections.label: Recapitulation · the opening theme returns
sections.mNote: opening theme returns in G major

cues.title: A slow introduction
cues.text: The symphony opens Adagio cantabile in 3/4, with oboes and bassoons over a held horn note, and strings joining within a few bars. It is a brief prelude: the Vivace assai will follow in about a minute and a half.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #546546, p. 1) shows oboes, bassoons and horn in the opening bars, with the strings entering soon after. The report shows a very quiet opening (−29.4 dB at 0:00) and its strongest boundary at 1:32, which marks the forte of the Vivace rather than the first bar of the new tempo; no entry is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Every Salomon symphony but one
cues.text: All of Haydn’s Salomon symphonies except No. 95 begin with a slow introduction, Orrin Howard notes. Howard calls the one here a brief, patrician prelude, with a passing grey cloud that darkens the horizon with sudden contrast.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s LA Phil programme note: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise. The note is a general description of the introduction; it does not time the cloud.

cues.title: The passing cloud
cues.text: At about 0:45 the harmony moves away from G major: the key estimate passes through F major and G minor, and then lands firmly on D major at a minute, the dominant. Compare the darker colour with the plain G major of the opening.
cues.evidence: Local key reads F major at 0:50 (r 0.58) and G minor at 0:55 (0.56), then D major at 1:00 (0.76) with a boundary at 1:00 (novelty 0.84). Estimates this tentative confirm only a darker region, not a chord.

cues.title: The introduction comes to rest
cues.text: The introduction ends on a dominant seventh chord, and the first violin leads out with a falling figure of eighth notes. Near 1:25 the sound almost disappears, one of the quietest windows of the movement. Listen to how little is left before the Vivace.
cues.evidence: Level falls to −30.4 dB at 1:20 and −39.7 dB at 1:25, among the quietest windows, then rises to −16.8 dB at 1:30. The dominant seventh close and the first violin’s falling eighth-note link are described in German Wikipedia (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)) and the score (IMSLP #546546, printed pp. 1–2); no general pause is claimed.

cues.title: Soft violins, then the full orchestra
cues.text: The 6/8 Vivace assai starts at about 1:28 with the two violins alone, piano, in a phrase that stays in the dominant region. Four bars later, at about 1:32, the full orchestra arrives forte on G. Howard hears the theme as whimsical, beginning mischievously outside the home key.
cues.evidence: The level is −16.8 dB at 1:30 and −8.2 dB at 1:35, with the strongest boundary at 1:32 (novelty 1.00): the large boundary follows the soft entry and marks the forte, not the first bar. The soft two-violin phrase, the dominant-region harmony and the tutti on the tonic in bar 22 are in German Wikipedia and the score (IMSLP #546546, printed p. 2); Howard’s description is at https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise. No bar is aligned.

cues.title: A London first night
cues.text: Haydn wrote the symphony in London in 1791 for his concert series with Salomon. It was first played at the Hanover Square Rooms on 23 March 1792, with Haydn leading from the fortepiano.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 94 article gives the 1791 composition in London, the premiere at the Hanover Square Rooms on 23 March 1792 and Haydn at the fortepiano: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._94_(Haydn).

cues.title: Three tunes in turn
cues.text: Howard lists the exposition’s cast of characters: the whimsical first theme, a lilting waltz tune, restrained and pure, and a warm melody with distinctive downward leaps. Listen for them in that order before the exposition ends.
cues.evidence: Howard’s description of the three themes (https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise); the report places D major from 1:40 to about 3:10 but cannot separate the tunes, so none is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening motif is worked
cues.text: At about 3:14 the development begins as a variant of the first theme, whose material is then spun on. Later, forte broken chords begin abruptly on A major and pass through D minor, B♭ and G minor. The report’s key estimates move through C major, D minor and B minor.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 3:14 (0.60), 3:20 (0.63) and 3:38 (0.74); local key reads G major at 3:15, C major at 3:20–3:30, D minor at 3:35–3:50 (r 0.62–0.88) and B minor at 4:00. German Wikipedia describes the development (bars 107–153) as a variant of the first theme spun on, then forte broken chords from bar 123 through A major, D minor, B♭ major and G minor. Bars are not aligned.

cues.title: The opening returns in G
cues.text: Around 4:10 the first theme comes back in G major. Haydn veils the return: after a cadence in B minor, repeated B’s sounding with G announce the tonic. The reprise begins like the exposition, but the two repeats of the first theme are missing. The recording matches the opening closely.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 93.0–110.5 s with 255.0–272.5 s (offset 162 s, no transposition, similarity 0.96); local key reads B minor at 4:00 and G major at 4:10–4:20 (r 0.73–0.81); the loudest windows include 4:20 and 4:35 (−8.1, −7.9 dB). The veiled return and the missing repeats are German Wikipedia’s description (bars 154 onward). The first bar of the return is not aligned.

cues.title: Pleyel, the rival
cues.text: Haydn told his biographer Griesinger that he wanted to surprise the public with something new and make a brilliant debut, so that his pupil Pleyel, then in London with a rival concert series, would not outdo him.
cues.evidence: Griesinger’s record of Haydn’s reply is quoted in Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 94 article (nickname section), which also names Pleyel’s concerts a week before Haydn’s: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._94_(Haydn). Howard’s LA Phil note gives the same context.

cues.title: A long return to G
cues.text: From about 5:15 the key estimate stays in G major for the rest of the movement. Just before it, between 4:55 and 5:10, the estimate reads D major.
cues.evidence: Local key reads D major at 4:55–5:10 (r 0.78–0.86) and G major from 5:15 to 6:05 (r 0.72–0.91); level falls to −20.3 dB at 5:15. Estimates confirm a region only.

cues.title: The final flourish
cues.text: At about 5:55 the orchestra begins its last tutti: detected attacks reach more than five per second at 6:00. Then the sound drops away to the end of the file at 6:10.
cues.evidence: Level is −12.1 dB at 5:55 and −9.7 dB at 6:00 with 5.2 attacks per second, then −40.0 dB at 6:05; the file ends at 6:10. The ending is not otherwise aligned to the score.

transitions.title: A hush, then the Vivace
transitions.how: The introduction closes on a dominant seventh chord, and the first violin leads out with a falling figure of eighth notes. The Vivace assai begins in 6/8, much faster than the 3/4 Adagio, with the two violins alone, piano, in a phrase that stays in the dominant region. Only four bars later does the full orchestra arrive, forte, on the tonic G. The tempo and metre change at the entry; the weight changes at the forte.
transitions.evidence: Level falls to −39.7 dB at 1:25, is −16.8 dB at 1:30 and rises to −8.2 dB at 1:35; the strongest boundary is 1:32 (1.00), which marks the forte rather than the first bar of the Vivace; D major is the local key at 1:00–1:15. The score changes from Adagio cantabile in 3/4 to Vivace assai in 6/8, with the soft two-violin phrase before the tutti (IMSLP #546546, printed pp. 1–2); no bar is aligned.

transitions.title: Leaving D major for the minor
transitions.how: The exposition has settled in D major, the dominant, for most of its length. The development begins as a variant of the first theme, and its material is spun on. Later, forte broken chords begin abruptly on A major and pass through D minor, B♭ major and G minor before a chromatic descent. The report’s estimates show the same departure from D: C major, then D minor by about 3:35 and B minor at 4:00.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 3:14 (0.60), 3:20 (0.63) and 3:38 (0.74); local key reads D major through 3:10, G major at 3:15, C major at 3:20–3:30 and D minor at 3:35–3:50. The keys are audio estimates; the score description is from German Wikipedia (bars 107–153). No bar is aligned.

transitions.title: The first theme comes home
transitions.how: The chromatic descent ends on F♯ major, the dominant of B minor, and a cadence in B minor follows. Repeated B’s, now sounding together with G, announce the tonic, so the return of the first theme in G is veiled rather than marked. The reprise then begins like the exposition, but without the two repeats of the first theme.
transitions.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 93.0–110.5 s with 255.0–272.5 s (similarity 0.96); local key reads B minor at 4:00, G major at 4:05–4:20; the loudest windows include 4:20 and 4:35. The F♯ major dominant, the B minor cadence and the veiled return are German Wikipedia’s description; the first bar of the return is not aligned.

source.title: Haydn, Symphony No. 94, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, ed. Rietz, plate 8876, [1855])
source.locator: IMSLP #546546, I. Adagio cantabile — Vivace assai, printed pp. 1–18; broad states only: times follow the report’s boundaries and the recurrence analysis and are approximate, and instrumental entries inside a state are not timed.

timeline.note: Oboes and bassoons sing the opening phrase over a held horn note; the strings join within a few bars, and a flute joins the wind motif when it is repeated.
Vivace assai: the two violins alone, piano, with the first phrase.
The full orchestra, with trumpets and timpani, arrives forte on the tonic.
The reprise: the first theme returns in G and the tutti, with trumpets and timpani, follows as in the exposition.

fields.note: The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 22 and 24 April 1929: the first side on 22 April, the second side on 24 April
fields.note: Young’s discography lists the first side (CVE-48983-2) with the 22 April 1929 session and the second side (CVE-48986-2) with a later recording date of 24 April 1929 for the published retaken side. DAHR’s list for 24 April 1929 includes CVE-48986 and Bolig gives take 2 for the second side. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
fields.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1: CVE-48983, take 2 (22 April 1929); side 2: CVE-48986, take 2 (24 April 1929)
fields.note: Young gives CVE-48983-2 and CVE-48986-2 as the issued takes of the first movement’s two sides. Bolig independently gives CVE-48986 take 2 for part 2. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Bob Varney — transfer from original Victor 78s

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files.
fields.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Haydn died in 1809. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
